BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120)

Pages 101–120 (20 pages)
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 101

development can occur. Think of a moment of seeing now — there are the colors that are sensed, the eyebase and the cakkhu-viññana (seeing consciousness). These three are each conditioned in various ways and yet they manage to come together briefly. No manager arranging this. It is happening now. Even at this intellectual level there is some understanding of the difference between concept and reality. Because there is a gradual shift in focus to the realities which underlie the conceptual world the complications in life are not taken quite as seriously as before. An analogy is watching a movie—fear, joy, excitement, anticipation, boredom— all these emotions may arise when sitting in front of the TV but we know it is just a show. A friend wrote to me:

Hi Robert, could you explain in a little more detail what should be done on a daily basis? Is it just a matter of recognition, as in ‘This is feeling…now this is intention…’, etc?

I mentioned the value of contemplation of the Dhamma and this is really the main part of what I do on a daily basis. There is some examination of what is appearing in the present moment, but it is very unmethodical. We might think contemplating (as in thinking) is a second rate practice and want to go directly to experiencing realities: And it is true that the intellectual understanding should eventually lead to direct awareness of whatever element is appearing. However, we should not underestimate the importance of reflecting on the teachings and comparing the Dhamma with what is arising here and now. It is a gradual process and even after satipaṭṭhāna arises there is

93

Page 101
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 102

needed more and more consideration of the teachings, and that supports more understanding, leading to more direct insight, a virtuous circle. This type of thinking comes with some degree of understanding and confidence and these mental factors can gradually grow, although it may still be, by and large, at the level of pariyatti. Returning to what I said about the ‘unmethodical’ examining of objects. Take an example: at the 5 sense doors there are only colour, sound, tangible object (hardness, heat etc), smell, taste (like sweet or sour) and when we reflect on these as they arise we may begin to see their ultimately insignificant nature. Instead of craving for something, there may be reflection that the object of seeing is only colour, nothing of substance; thus there is a start in differentiating reality from concept. Another example: if irritation with someone/something arises we might remember that this is simply dosa, a conditioned element. If we have studied Abhidhamma there are different thoughts that might arise along with this: ‘There was seeing and visible object, hearing and sound and then there were the many mind door processes. None of them are self’. While thinking in this way dosa has already fallen away and is replaced by an interest in the process itself… But there are many other trains of thought related to Dhamma that might also occur. Thus not rote recitation, it will to some extent depend on what aspect of Dhamma we have been reading or thinking about. It is the nature of the mind to do this— to contemplate what we have heard. Simple in a way but because it pertains to the understanding of reality, to namas and rupas, it is so deep. Sometimes it stops at mere remembering or it may go further to condition investigation of the present moment in relation to what has been remembered. It is all natural—ordinary even. Or

94

Page 102
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 103

there may be no wise reflection at all — ignorance, aversion and greed may dominate for long periods simply because they are conditioned to arise. We may go for long periods without any contemplation, engrossed in the conceptual world, and that is the nature of the busy layman’s life. The texts speak about deeper levels where the objects arising at the sense doors are apprehended as being six different worlds.

Nina van Gorkom: Those who develop vipassana will know what the world really is; they will know that there are “six worlds”: the world of visible object, of sound, of odour, of flavour, of tangible objects and of mental objects. They will know that these worlds are impermanent. Buddhism in Daily Life

Acceptance Another aspect of developing vipassana is acceptance of the moment as it is. From the satipaṭṭhāna sutta we see that any reality is viable as an object for understanding. It doesn’t matter if greed arises or anger, confusion or great insight, pleasant feeling, unpleasant feeling, heat or cold, whether we are in the toilet, looking left or right, keeping silent or talking.

And how, O bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu live contemplating consciousness in consciousness? Here, O bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands the consciousness with lust, as with lust; the consciousness without lust, as without lust; the consciousness with hate, as with hate; the consciousness without hate, as without hate. Satipaṭṭhāna sutta

95

Page 103
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 104

This interest in the present moment is very subtle. The slightest wish for a ‘better’ object moves us away from the present moment. Perhaps we unknowingly desire more clarity or think ‘the consciousness with lust’ is shameful; and if so we are no longer understanding the moment as it really is. If satipaṭṭhāna develops there is growing acceptance of whatever arises, it comes with a special type of calm. Understanding of the four jati- vipaka citta, kiriya citta, akusala citta and kusala citta - also helps. Vipaka citta such as seeing or hearing are the result of kamma from the past. Body consciousness (another type of vipaka) experiences tangible object such as heat or hardness and the accompanying feeling can be pleasant or painful. However, this is separate from any attachment or aversion (these are the jati of akusala) that arises so quickly afterwards. Those moments of vipaka arising at the 5 sense doors can be thought of as passive - vitakka (translated as ‘thinking’) does not accompany the five pairs which are seeing, hearing, etc. Thus so different from the moments of kusala and akusala citta.

Two types of worldling There are two types of putthujjjana (worlding), the andhaputthujjana and the kalyanaputthujjana. The kalyanaputthujjana is working towards deeper understanding.

The Enlightened One, the kinsman of the sun, Speaks of the worldling in a twofold way: One is the worldling blinded by darkness, The other the worldling noble and good. The blind worldling (andhaputhujjana) is the worldling who has not studied, interrogated, learned, memorized, and reviewed the teachings on the aggre96

Page 104
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 105

gates, elements, sense bases, etc. The worldling who has done so is the good worldling (kalyāṇaputhujjana). Commentary to the Brahmajala sutta, translation Bodhi, All Embracing Net of Views, p.111

Also Commentary to Mulapariyaya sutta (translated by bhikkhu Bodhi as Discourse on the Root of Existence).

The ‘uninstructed worldling’ needs to be taught, because he possesses neither learning (agama) nor achievement. For he who possesses neither the learning running counter to the activity of conceiving because he has neglected to study, question, and discriminate the aggregates (khandhas), elements, sense bases (ayatanas) truths, law of conditionality and foundations of mindfulness etc, nor spiritual achievement because he has failed to achieve what should be achieved by practice is said to be ‘uninstructed’. (p.40)

It is a gradual process that begins with study and reflection on the teachings. From the Satipaṭṭhāna sutta:

The Four Kinds of Clear Comprehension And further, O bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, in going forwards (and) in going backwards, is a person practicing clear comprehension; in looking straight on (and) in looking away from the front, is a person practicing clear comprehension; in bending and in stretching, is a person practicing clear comprehension; in wearing the shouldercloak, the (other two) robes (and) the bowl, is a person

97

Page 105
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 106

practicing clear comprehension; in regard to what is eaten, drunk, chewed and savored, is a person practicing clear comprehension; in defecating and in urinating, is a person practicing clear comprehension; in walking, in standing (in a place), in sitting (in some position), in sleeping, in waking, in speaking and in keeping silence, is a person practicing clear comprehension.

The Satipaṭṭhāna sutta commentary gives an example of this:

The Elder Tipitaka Maha Siva indeed said: Who, after walking or exercising long in the ambulatory, stands and reflects: ‘The bodily and mental things which existed during the time of exercises on the ambulatory ended just there on the ambulatory,’ is called a doer of clear comprehension in walking.

And:

He who whilst speaking thinks: ‘This sound arises dependent on the lips, teeth, tongue, palate, and the act of the mind that accords to that sound,’ speaks, mindful and clearly comprehending.

Question: Studying the Dhamma seems to be within my sphere of control. I believe you said that we are lucky enough to find the Dhamma due to our past interest and progress in previous lives. If so, wasn’t that activity somehow efficacious in bringing about a favourable result?

That interest and resultant activity is all by various conditions

98

Page 106
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 107

-without any need to posit a self. It is not that one day one is filled with wrong view and next some Damascus moment and all wrong view disappears. It is incremental, cira kala bhavana, long time development. And that is the way it is; better to be going slowly in the right direction than fast in the wrong.

Udana 5.5 In the same way in this teaching and training the penetration to enlightenment comes from gradual training, progress, and practice, not abruptly.

So what should be done assuming one has studied and begun to understand the meaning of the teachings:

Sariputta my friend, which things should a virtuous monk attend to in an appropriate way? A virtuous monk, Kotthita my friend, should attend in an appropriate way to the five clinging-aggregates as inconstant, stressful, a disease, a cancer, an arrow, painful, an affliction, alien, a dissolution, an emptiness, not-self. Which five? Form as a clinging-aggregate, feeling… perception… fabrications… consciousness as a clinging-aggregate. A virtuous monk should attend in an appropriate way to these five clinging-aggregates as inconstant, stressful, a disease, a cancer, an arrow, painful, an affliction, alien, a dissolution, an emptiness, not-self. For it is possible that a virtuous monk, attending in an appropriate way to these five clinging-aggregates as inconstant… not-self, would realize the fruit of streamentry. Then which things should an arahant attend to in an

99

Page 107
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 108

appropriate way? An arahant [also] should attend in an appropriate way to these five clinging-aggregates as inconstant, stressful, a disease, a cancer, an arrow, painful, an affliction, alien, a dissolution, an emptiness, not-self. Saṁyutta Nikāya 22.122 Silavant Sutta

Further:

And what is the development of concentration that leads to the destruction of the taints? Here, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating arising and vanishing in the five aggregates subject to clinging: ‘Such is form, such its origin, such its passing away; such is feeling … such is perception … such are volitional activities … such is consciousness, Numerical such its origin, such its passing away.’ Sayings 41(1)

This advanced level of understanding where the rise and fall is directly known can’t occur unless there has been enough prior understanding, firstly at the level of pariyatti, the intellectual understanding. With regard to understanding the usual distinctions are pariyatti, patipatti and pativedha. A similar classification is saccā-ñāṇa (sacca-nana), kicca-ñāṇa and katañāṇa. Sacca-nana is a level of understanding where the pariyatti (intellectual level) is very firm (in some contexts it has a wider meaning). One has real conviction of the noble truths and so on. This level is a foundation for higher understanding. The application of Dhamma is to learn to study the khandhas, the ayatanas, the dhatus. So satipaṭṭhāna is about learning to see wisely that there are only conditioned moments of

100

Page 108
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 109

materiality and mentality: seeing is arising now, thinking is arising now, feeling, hardness, softness, heat, interest, sound, colour, boredom, happiness and so on. All of these moments arising now have their own nature but they also all cease instantly and new ones replace them. This can be seen to some degree, sometimes, and it concurs exactly with what is said in the texts. Thus there is a breaking down of what we took as ‘something’ into what is really present. And what is present is merely these elements.

Motivation and lost drive

Someone wrote: Since learning about Buddhism I have lost much of what little drive I had before to have a career, family or even friendships as they usually involve idle chatter and drinking intoxicants.

Actually family, friendships and career improve with right understanding. For example, if there is some understanding about conditionality there must be more patience with children, wife and friends. There will be more understanding of the difference between attachment and metta. As far as career goes, it is not really unbridled ambition that leads to success but instead taking on the tasks that need to be done and doing them carefully and willingly—and that attitude is supported by Dhamma insights. Of course it takes time to understand what anatta really means but correctly/wisely seeing that all dhammas are not self, sabbe dhamma anatta, is highly beneficial. It makes life easier because it shines light everywhere. Views If we find ourselves thinking that any of the khandhas can last,

101

Page 109
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 110

or we think there is a self then that is wrong view showing itself there and then. Or maybe we think that there is no rebirth. We can know that is not what the Buddha taught. Perhaps before we started to study Dhamma we didn’t think giving was particularly meritorious. Or we were disrespectful to our parents. So we start to see what is meant by ditthujukamma, straightening of views. This level of right understanding is not yet satipaṭṭhāna but it is a prerequisite for the direct understanding. And of course this becomes more and more refined. Or it doesn’t—one might resist what the Buddha taught, or read into it other ideas.

Saṁyutta Nikāya, Salayatana Samyutta 55 (3) Uprooting the Fetters Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, for the fetters to be uprooted? Bhikkhu, when one knows and sees the eye as nonself, the fetters are uprooted. When one knows and sees forms as nonself … (all as above) … When one knows and sees thus, bhikkhu, the fetters are uprooted. Connected Discourses

Samatha bhavana and Vipassana bhavana

Aṅguttara Nikāya 11.12.2. Recollection with Mahānāma Mahānāma, you should develop this recollection of the Buddha while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. You should develop it while engaged in work and while living at home in a house full of children [repeats for other recollections].

Mahanama had already reached a stage of enlightenment and

102

Page 110
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 111

thus his recollections of the six objects would be easily fruitful. But anyone who has confidence in the Dhamma can also benefit. And it doesn’t need to be especially systematic (which can morph into ‘tedious’). When we are considering aspects of the Dhamma that can be also Dhammānussati (Dhammanusati) as there is appreciation of the Dhamma. Another sutta mentions that many laypeople still enjoying sense pleasures can develop deep insight.

The Greater Discourse to Vacchagotta ‘’Vaccha, not one, not one hundred, not two hundred, not three hundred, not four hundred, not five hundred. There are many more female lay disciples of mine wearing white clothes lead the holy life, while partaking sensual pleasures, doing the work in the dispensation have dispelled doubts. Have become confident of what should and should not be done. They do not need a teacher any more in the dispensation of the Teacher.” MN 73 Mahavacchagotta Sutta

Thus we read in the suttas of bhikkhus, bhikkhunis, laymen and laywomen attaining stages of enlightenment. Some bhikkhus frequented secluded forests, others recited, discussed and contemplated in busy monastic centers. There were laymen and women who were celibate, living lives of simplicity; and others who were married and indulging in sense pleasures. Today I was listening to a translation of a sutta about dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) while watching my children swimming. At different times I was in admiration of the Dhamma, of the Buddha who discovered it, and the Sangha who preserved it. We should be aware though that simply bringing

103

Page 111
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 112

to mind one of the recollections (Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha, our virtue, our generosity, and virtues of the devas) is not a guarantee of kusala citta. Regarding the development of satipaṭṭhāna, this depends on correct intellectual understanding of Dhamma. There should be understanding of the void nature of the world (suññata), that everything is ceasing immediately. We may make effort to see the present moment but with the idea of a person who is doing so, unaware that what we are trying to be aware of is already past. Right effort arises with panna (wisdom) and with detachment—it is not merely a matter of bringing attention to an object. Kusala citta can’t be forced to arise.

Difference between samatha and vipassana

The Visuddhimagga explains that one intent on development of samatha: should sever any of the ten impediments that he may have. A dwelling, family, and gain, A class, and building too as fifth, And travel, kin, affliction, books, and supernormal powers: ten. Vism. III 29. […] Iddhi, here, means the supernormal powers of a worldling. It is difficult to manage—like a child lying on its back or like tender young crops. It can be broken even by a small thing. However, it is an obstacle to vipassanā (insight), though not to samādhi (concentration), because it is something attainable after attaining concentration. Therefore, for one intent on insight, the obstruction of supernormal powers should be removed; for the other [i.e., one aiming at concentration], it may be left as it is.

104

Page 112
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 113

Vism. iii 56

This can help us see the different ways of insight and samatha. For those who develop samatha superpowers are not an impediment as iddhi are a result of samatha. But all the other nine: the ‘dwelling, family, and gain, a class, and building too as fifth, And travel, kin, affliction, books’ are impediments. [Note, that as I mentioned earlier the six recollections can be developed in a busy daily life]. However, for the one who is developing vipassana it is reversed, as the way of insight can be developed even in the midst of all these nine. Why is it indicated that only the iddhi are impediments to vipassana? It is because of their fragility that one would have to be so careful to maintain them, it distracts from the main goal.

You say that vipassana can be developed in daily life. My job is demanding and when I am trying to solve the issues at work I am not thinking about Dhamma at all.

When we are fully preoccupied with worldly matters, as we often are, at those times there is not development of intellectual understanding (pariyatti). This is the way things are. Nevertheless, there may be opportunities that can arise naturally to reflect on Dhamma or even have direct insight, if only for a few moments. There may be some understanding of hardness or that thinking goes on naturally by itself. These moments can come unexpectedly.

Shouldn’t we set aside quiet periods to devote to bhavana, insight meditation.

105

Page 113
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 114

Anytime we spend contemplating the Dhamma is beneficial. I certainly appreciate those minutes and hours when I can read a section of the Tipitaka or ponder at leisure the teachings. We need to be careful though that we are not closing off the possibility of understanding arising at other times. Also we should be awake to the possibility of self-deception. If we don’t have enough understanding at the level of pariyatti then what we are calling ‘insight meditation’ might not qualify. And even if we are well versed in the texts we should be patient and place the principles of anatta to the fore: sati and wisdom don’t arise at anyone’s will.

The right attitude when studying the Dhamma

One who Dwells in the Dhamma 74(4): It is said, Bhante, ‘one who dwells in the Dhamma, one who dwells in the Dhamma.’ In what way is a bhikkhu one who dwells in the Dhamma? (1) Here, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu learns the Dhamma—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, quotations, birth stories, amazing accounts, and questions-and-answers—but he does not go further and understand its meaning with wisdom. This is called a bhikkhu who is absorbed in learning, not one who dwells in the Dhamma. (2) Again, a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard and learned it, but he does not go further and understand its meaning with wisdom. This is called a bhikkhu who is absorbed in communication, not one who dwells in the Dhamma. (3) Again, a bhikkhu recites the Dhamma in detail as

106

Page 114
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 115

he has heard it and learned it, but he does not go further and understand its meaning with wisdom. This is called a bhikkhu who is absorbed in recitation, not one who dwells in the Dhamma. (4) Again, a bhikkhu ponders, examines, and mentally inspects the Dhamma as he has heard it and learned it, but he does not go further and understand its meaning with wisdom. This is called a bhikkhu who is absorbed in thought, not one who dwells in the Dhamma. (5) Here, a bhikkhu learns the Dhamma—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, quotations, birth stories, amazing accounts, and questions-and-answers—but he goes further and understands its meaning with wisdom. It is in this way that a bhikkhu is one who dwells in the Dhamma. The Numerical Discourses.

The Commentary to this sutta notes that the one who ‘goes further and understands its meaning with wisdom’ refers to attainment of the paths with insight. The sutta shows that only learning Dhamma is not enough. There needs to be further effort to penetrate the meaning.

Question: when I read the Abhidhamma or suttas talking about aggregates and sense bases and dependent origination it seems overly complicated. I think it is easier to choose a technique and follow that.

It may seem easier but is it leading in the right direction. The Dhamma is profound and not easily grasped. If it were a matter of following a technique then that would have been the main

107

Page 115
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 116

focus of what the Buddha taught for all those years.

More on ‘Method’

Connected Discourses 153 (8) Is There a Method? “Is there a method of exposition, bhikkhus, by means of which a bhikkhu—apart from faith, apart from personal preference, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned reflection, apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it can declare final knowledge thus: ‘Destroyed is birth, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being’? […] There is a method of exposition by means of which a bhikkhu— apart from faith … apart from acceptance of a view after pondering it—can declare final knowledge thus: ‘Destroyed is birth … there is no more for this state of being.’ And what is that method of exposition? Here, bhikkhus, having seen a form with the eye, if there is lust, hatred, or delusion internally, a bhikkhu understands: ‘There is lust, hatred, or delusion internally’; or, if there is no lust, hatred, or delusion internally, he understands: ‘There is no lust, hatred, or delusion internally.’ Since this is so, are these things to be understood by faith, or by personal preference, or by oral tradition, or by reasoned reflection, or by acceptance of a view after pondering it? No, venerable sir.

Vañcaka (Cheating) Dhammas

T hey have the appearance of kusala (wholesomeness) but are subtle types of akusala. They are explained in the Commentary to the Nettipakarana. Here are some examples:

• One feels aversion to the daily grind but thinks this is a sign of genuine renunciation. (Renunciation as a mental factor always comes with either pleasant of neutral feeling, never unpleasant). • One has desire for progress and doesn’t see the lobha (tanha) that is there. This is just spinning the wheel of dependent origination all the faster. • Or one does nothing at all - and thinks this is wholesome ‘patience’. • One has dislike for some people (akusala) and avoids meeting them. This looks like kusala in the sense that also seclusion can be kusala. • Or one dislikes working but thinks he is being virtuous by avoiding work so that he can ‘do Dhamma’.

110

Page 118
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 119

• One disputes with others but thinks that that is kusala because he is ‘teaching them real Dhamma’. • One has doubts about Dhamma. But it can masquerade as ‘reflection’ as he turns it around in his mind, and gets enamored with it. • Or one disagrees with aspects of the teaching and searches for other teachings that are more amenable - they think this is Dhamma-vicaya. (It can be done rightly if the teaching they prefer is more suited to their nature without rejecting the other aspects). • Or one knows sila or generosity or respect are important so they focus on only these (neglecting other areas) but with a subtle idea that ‘this is the path’. Or he neglects sila and dana because ‘panna is more important’. • One has strong attachment to some teacher and thinks this is saddha in the Dhamma. • One memorizes deep teachings like sabbe sanhara anicca. They think it is the pariyatti level of understanding. But this can be mere sanna, concentration and citta without any real intellectual understanding, so it is not yet pariyatti.

These outward actions can also be done with genuine kusala, so they can be hard to detect even by the person engaging in them.

111

Page 119
October 29 2025A Path Without Ownership Standard Print Ready BHAVANA IN DAILY LIFE (p. 101–120) p. 120

13

Viññanam anidassanam

There is no consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and that will remain the same just like eternity itself. Connected Discourses on the Aggregates 22:96

T he rather rare phrase, viññanam anidassanam, gained some prominence in recent years. The reason to add this chapter is that some of the explanations about it are serious deviations from Theravada. First there is a example of this misinterpretation followed with quotes from several Pāḷi scholars who explain the correct understanding.

Consciousness without surface Thanissaro writes: (vinnanam anidassanam): This term appears to be related to the following image from SN 12.64: “Just as if there were a roofed house or a roofed hall having windows on the north, the south, or the east.

112

Page 120
